summary: This memo updates the SSH specifications by defining a way for clients and servers to tell each other which protocol extensions they support. The exchange happens after key exchange, so it is confidential.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC gives SSH clients and servers a way to tell each other which optional extensions they support. They exchange the information after key exchange, so the message is protected by the SSH session.

subtitle: A confidential way for SSH clients and servers to exchange supported protocol extensions.

tldr.problem: SSH had no general extension exchange, making it difficult to discover peer capabilities without risking a failed attempt.
tldr.mechanism: Client and server signal support in SSH_MSG_KEXINIT, then can exchange named extension values in SSH_MSG_EXT_INFO after key exchange.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines four extensions and creates a registry for future names. It updates RFCs 4251, 4252, 4253 and 4254; RFC 9519 later updates it.

today: RFC 8308 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFCs 4251, 4252, 4253 and 4254. It is updated by RFC 9519.

sections.title: Why SSH Needs Extension Exchange
sections.content:
The original SSH transport protocol did not define a general way to exchange extension support. Some implementations also reject unrecognized information, so trying an unknown feature could cause a connection to fail.

One motivation was allowing a client to learn which public-key algorithms a server accepts before trying an authentication method. This can avoid failed attempts that some servers treat as suspicious.
sections.plainLanguage: A client should be able to learn what a server supports before trying a feature. The extension exchange provides that information without trial and error.

sections.title: Signaling Support During Key Exchange
sections.content:
In the first SSH_MSG_KEXINIT, a server adds ext-info-s and a client adds ext-info-c to the key-exchange algorithm list. The names differ so they cannot accidentally select a new key-exchange algorithm.

A party that sends its indicator must be ready to accept SSH_MSG_EXT_INFO from its peer. Either side may send the message when the peer has signaled support, but neither side is required to send one.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side adds a role-specific marker to its opening key-exchange message. The marker says it can process an extension list from the peer.

sections.title: The SSH_MSG_EXT_INFO Message
sections.content:
SSH_MSG_EXT_INFO has message value 7, a count of extensions, and that number of name and binary-value pairs. Each extension defines how its name and value work.

Receivers ignore unknown extension names and their values. They must tolerate any byte sequence in an unknown value, including null bytes, and must ignore the order in which extensions appear.
sections.plainLanguage: The message is a counted list of extension names and values. A receiver skips names it does not recognize and tolerates their values.

sections.title: When Extensions Are Exchanged
sections.content:
A client that sends SSH_MSG_EXT_INFO sends it as the next packet after its first SSH_MSG_NEWKEYS. A server may send it immediately after its first SSH_MSG_NEWKEYS, just before SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_SUCCESS, at both times or not at all.

The later message lets a server withhold some information until the client authenticates. If a second server message is sent, it replaces the earlier extension list. A client that signaled support must accept either timing but cannot require the message.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends its list immediately after the first keys are active. The server can send its list then or wait until just before successful authentication.

sections.title: Four Initial Extensions
sections.content:
server-sig-algs lists public-key algorithms the server can process for authentication. delay-compression lets both sides choose compression that starts after authentication, without another key exchange.

no-flow-control can disable channel window limits when both parties support it, and allows no more than one simultaneous channel. elevation lets a client request whether an administrative session should be elevated or use the server default.
sections.plainLanguage: The first extensions cover accepted signature algorithms, delayed compression, channel flow control and administrative elevation. Each extension has its own rules for when it takes effect.

sections.title: Compatibility, Security and Names
sections.content:
Extension negotiation happens after key exchange, so extension messages are confidential. The server may also wait until authentication before revealing an extension. The RFC says the security considerations of the base SSH architecture still apply.

IANA registered message values 7 and 8, the two key-exchange indicators and an Extension Names registry. New non-local extension names require IETF Review. The RFC also notes an incompatibility in OpenSSH clients through version 7.5 with null bytes in extension values.
sections.plainLanguage: The extension list is sent after the SSH keys are in place. An official name registry helps different implementations use the same name for each extension.
